articles.title: Show HN: DBDelve – Open-Source DB Client Made with Rust and GPUI
articles.summary:
Hi HN, I’m Shayan and a few months ago I started building a DB Client DBDelve with a focus on performance and just making something that feels good to use (in the spirit of Zed, Ghostty, and other tools that just feel pleasant to use).
For my workflow I’ve always looked for performance, especially since some time ago I had a really outdated machine and any kind of bloat was really noticeable, I remember using DBeaver and it just crashing on me multiple times, I also had to use postGIS which just made it worse. I migrated all my essential dev tools to use the ones with performance in mind (Zed, Ghostty etc) but the only thing that was missing was DB Client. The main choices everyone has are DBeaver which is a memory hog and an overkill for most of the tasks imo. The other options like Datagrid, Beekeeper, TablePlus are either electron based so bloated and memory hogs or paid and closed-source.
DBDelve 0.3.6 against DBeaver 25.3.1 on the same Postgres table, median of 5 runs each (2026-10-11, M1 Pro, 32 GB). Times are from the action to the rows rendered.
                            DBDelve   DBeaver
  Launch                    1.1 s     5.2 s
  Idle memory               133 MB    606 MB
  1,000-row query           0.21 s    1.96 s
  1M rows, time             56 s      208 s
  1M rows, memory [1]       4.9 GB    17 GB

Scrolling perf with 1 million rows loaded with 100 columns each: https://youtu.be/V2MOhJYFqIE
It has most of the features most devs would need for 90% of their workflow plus some more I thought would be a nice touch:
Readonly, read-write and Full Access modes
Glass themes (If you’re into them, I am)
Keyboard focused with every keybinding customizable
Organization of connections into projects
Me and some other folks have been daily driving it for more than a month now and most good feedback comes on it having a really simple UI to navigate, very stable for its age and the performance of course. I’m also sharing here because those people tell me this has potential to grow so I’m trying my hand at distributing it.
Just want to give a huge shoutout here to the Zed team for GPUI, it's a breeze to work with if you just get through them not updating the crate officially on crates.io but the community has found the solutions for it, you just have to dig deep for it. It performs extremely well and just the HTML-like structure of it, makes it easy to understand for someone from a web dev background and agents are very good at writing it too. GPUI component also solves a lot of problems with having a good component library we can use. I think for anyone starting a GPUI project now, GPUI-kit makes a lot of sense, it just bundles GPUI, GPUI-component together and has some optimizations adding retained mode which is experimental but could provide a lot of benefit, so think all things considered it should be the default way.
The major optimization I did was just lowering the memory overhead by using packed rows which reduced the memory usage by 40% on large datasets (8.1GB to 4.9GB on a 4GB table loaded in app), everything else came bundled in with Rust and GPUI mostly or they just made it very easy.
Limitations:
It's not signed and notarized, identity verification from apple's side has been a nightmare but it should be signed soon.
Don’t expect feature parity with more mature clients for now, the general direction of this right now is the zed way of adding features in but after making sure the core workflows are done with a high quality.
Do give it a try, you can import your connections from dbeaver and tableplus.

Mr. Rubio’s memo was circulated to administration officials with
high-level security clearances ahead of a trip Mr. Trump took to
China in May, the people briefed on the matter said. They spoke on
the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive material.
Despite his status as an A.I. pioneer and head of one of the
world’s most valuable companies, Mr. Huang was initially left off
the list of major business and tech executives invited to join Mr.
Trump in China. It is unclear whether the exclusion was connected
to the memo. By that point, a number of people inside the
administration were concerned about Mr. Huang’s influence on the
president’s policy of only lightly regulating A.I., people
briefed on the matter said.
After Mr. Trump saw media coverage about Mr. Huang being absent
from the delegation, the president asked him to join the
trip by meeting Air Force One during a layover in Alaska. The
president drafted a social media post saying that it was an honor
to have “the Great Jensen Huang,” and other business leaders
“journeying to the Great Country of China where I will be asking
President Xi, a Leader of extraordinary distinction, to ‘open up’
China so that these brilliant people can work their magic.”
This Huang-Huang affair explains a few things that until now didn’t make sense, and Jensen Huang not being invited on that May trip to China — until Trump invited him on the fly at the Alaska layover — is one of them. Also worth noting that on multi-byline stories, The Times puts them in order of who contributed the most to the story. In this case it’s Haberman, who is closest to Trump and the White House:
Asked about Mr. Huang’s admission to his company about his affair
with Ms. Huang, Mr. Trump told reporters on Sunday evening that he
did not regret his own lack of action.
“No, I don’t think so,” the president said. He added that he
believed Mr. Huang should stay on as Nvidia’s chief executive.
“I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse
for it. You have to hear it,” Mr. Trump said.
Trump, you will recall, was convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records related to his hush-money payments to porno star Stormy Daniels, who banged him and (spanked him with a magazine on which he was on the cover) at a celebrity golf tournament in Lake Tahoe in 2006. That was four months after Melania Trump, his third wife, gave birth to their son Barron. So take “he probably has an excuse for it” with a $130,000 grain of salt.
There’s a Journalism 101 adage that news stories should be written in an “upside down triangle”, with the most important information at the top and the least important at the bottom. Another little inside-baseball tidbit about The Times, however, is that The Times, rather uniquely, often buries the most interesting (but not most important) paragraph at the very end. This story ends thus:
In recent years, Megaspeed, despite having essentially a
storefront office and little local footprint, purchased $2
billion worth of Nvidia’s products. Megaspeed builds data centers
in Southeast Asia that rent out their computing power to Alibaba,
the giant Chinese internet company. U.S. officials suspect
Megaspeed has been helping smuggle restricted advanced Nvidia
chips into China.
If true, this is politically damaging to both Nvidia and Huang personally, but the context is that Nvidia booked over $300 billion in revenue over the last year.

articles.title: Optimal virulence and the Android lockdown
articles.summary:
When you get a cold, the virus hijacks your cells and uses them to make copies of itself, destroying the cells in the process. The virus does not care about you. And yet, if you get a cold, your body doesn’t dissolve into a pile of virus-enriched goo as a result of all your cells disregarding survival to focus on virus manufacturing.
Why? Well, you have an immune system. But also, if that did happen, other people would say, “Oh no, Alice has dissolved into a pile of virus-enriched goo; we should stay away lest we also become goo piles.” Better to just hijack some of your cells, so you can walk around and spread the virus to other people. Thus, the theory of optimal virulence says that a more laid-back cold virus will be more successful in the long run, which is why the cold viruses that thrive today are the non-goo-pile-converting kind.
Anyway. Most people reading this have paid Apple $400-$1600 for a phone on which you can’t do anything without Apple’s permission and monitoring. That was a strange decision, but on Android phones you can run whatever you want. For example, I noticed a couple of months ago that all RSS apps were terrible, so I spent 15 long minutes having AI make me a non-terrible one. I copied the file to my phone, installed it, and entered RSS nirvana, no registration, no app store, no nothing. It seems ludicrous that I wouldn’t be able to do that.
And yet, Google plans to change things. Soon, you won’t be able to run any app on an Android phone unless the person who made it bends the knee by paying a fee, giving Google their government ID, listing all apps they’ve ever made, etc. There will be an “escape hatch” for users to install other apps, but it involves secret menus and scary warnings and a 24-hour waiting period. Google says they’re doing this for security reasons, to prevent people from installing malware that does things like steal financial information.
Three things that any credible analysis of this situation must acknowledge
The security issue is real, and this change will help. Lots of people are in fact getting tricked into installing malware on their phones, and common sense says that this will accelerate with AI. Common sense also says that during that 24-hour waiting period, some of those people might wonder if it’s really normal for OfficialMicrosoftSupportProfessional021 to contact them on WhatsApp to send totally-safe-virus-scanner.apk. It would be convenient for lockdown opponents if the security issue was fake, but it isn’t.
For 95% of people reading this, these restrictions would not be a big deal. You click a few buttons, wait 24 hours once, and then you have the same freedom you have now. That’s still far better than Apple phones where there is no process at all. Oddly, it’s also better than Apple computers, where installing programs from non-verified developers has all sorts of friction that can never be removed. Most people I know use Apple computers anyway and just tolerate the indignity.
If Google cared about freedom or privacy, they could have achieved their security goals without as much harm to freedom or privacy. For example, instead instead of making themselves the sole arbiter, they could have allowed for multiple certifying entities, and could have allowed users to add others (perhaps after a 24-hour waiting period). Arguably, that would be more secure: That way, grandma could install my RSS app without leaving herself open to random malware. Or, Google could have used private on-device malware scanning, or lots of other things. Google didn’t do that because they don’t care about freedom and privacy and because they like money.1
I think that’s a fair summary. This change addresses a real issue, but it does so in a self-serving way that needlessly destroys freedom. Even so, it only destroys a bit of freedom. This change, by itself, isn’t really a huge deal.
Reading between the lines, I think the real concern is what this might portend. Having made this change, maybe Google will gradually add further restrictions, slowly boiling the frog and moving ever-closer to an Apple-style dictatorship.
But will they? Maybe! Still, this whole situation seems under-theorized. There are good reasons to think that a full lockdown would not be in Google’s interest. And if you care about digital freedom, you could argue that a full lockdown would be a good thing.
Some other analogies
Switching insurance sucks, so some insurers offer a low initial rate and then gradually raise it over time. But they don’t want to raise it too much. Maybe they can charge you $50 more per year than a competitor, because it’s not worth your time to switch to save $50. But if they tried to charge you $5000 more per year, you’d be gone.
Or try this: Say it’s 1750 AD and you’re the King of France. You care nothing about your subjects and only want to extract the maximum possible loot for yourself, no offense Louis XV. How high should you set taxes? High, because you want loot. But not too high, because you don’t want your subjects to revolt and kill you. But still pretty high, because revolting is hard, and your subject know that even if they succeed, they might just end up with another ruler that’s just as rapacious as you.
Or: Say you put a frog in a pot of water and slowly heat it up. What do you think actually happens?
Back to phones
Why are there no Linux phones?
OK, technically there are Linux phones. There are various Linux phone operating systems (PureOS, postmarketOS, Mobian, Manjaro Mobile, Fedora Mobility, openSUSE Mobile) as well as sorta-Linux-sorta-Android operating systems (Ubtuntu touch, Droidian, FuriOS, Sailfish OS) and manufacturers who support them (Purism, Pine, Fairphone, Shift, FuriLabs, {J,V}olla). While I love and support these (♡), the general consensus is that they don’t currently offer an experience that’s remotely comparable to stock Android or iOS, especially for the price.
(Even more technically, Android is itself a kind of Linux, but you know what I mean.)
Obviously, the laws of physics do not forbid Linux phones from being just as good and cheap as an Android phone. They currently aren’t because:
Making cheap phones requires huge economies of scale.
Making a good operating system requires a huge amount of work.
For a phone to be useful it needs good apps, which requires a huge amount of work.
Linux phones don’t have those economies of scale because few people buy them. So, there isn’t enough money to pay people to perfect the operating systems, and most companies don’t bother making apps, and so few people buy those phones.
Meanwhile, there are also various Android-except-de-Googled phone operating systems (LineageOS, GrapheneOS, /e/OS, CalyxOS), and the consensus is that these do come reasonably close to the experience of stock Android or iOS.
Personally, I used Android for a long time while trying to disable as much of Google’s apps and telemetry as I could. A while ago, I got fed up with this and switched to Graphene, one of the most popular Android-except-de-Googled variants. I don’t enjoy tech support bullshit, so I expected some pain, but I was willing to tolerate it for freedom/privacy/whatever. In practice, I found that everything was easy and worked flawlessly and there was no pain at all. Using Graphene made me realize that I had forgotten what it feels like to be “respected” by technology.
So, on a personal level, I recommend that you use Graphene. But this whole situation is full of weird tensions. For one thing, the Graphene project depends on Google for the base of their operating system, and only really survives because of Google’s tolerance. And, at the moment, the only way to use Graphene is to… buy a phone made by Google.
And while I recommend you use Graphene, what I’d prefer you do is switch to a true Linux phone. That would mean that you pay a lot of money for a poor phone experience. But it would help grow the Linux phone ecosystem. If enough people did that, then Linux phones might become become good enough that selfish people like me would switch, further growing the Linux phone ecosystem, et cetera.
That seems unlikely, because digital freedom weirdos face a collective action problem: Linux phones are bad and people are selfish, so we keep buying Android phones and Linux phones stay bad.
There are two ways to solve that collective action problem. Either some entity could invest a ton of money to make Linux phones good, or some entity could do something to make Android worse.
The status quo is good for Google
You may already see the argument I’m making here. Currently Android is just open enough that weirdos like me can run a variant that gives us most of what we want. But doing that is annoying enough that 99.9% of people don’t. This gives Google almost all the benefits of full control, while also sucking up all the oxygen and preventing a real alternative from emerging.
(Apple, incidentally, is laughing. They get to enjoy a full dictatorship while Google does all the hard work.)
Suppose that in six months, Google decides to escalate the lockdown and completely removes the ability to run independent apps. What then?
In the short-run, not much. Tech freedom weirdos would howl, normies wouldn’t notice, and the world would keep turning. But let’s look at some numbers. A rough estimate is that 3-5 million people currently use private de-Googled Android variants like Lineage or Graphene. That’s a crisp 0.1% of the global Android market. Meanwhile, it’s thought that 300-500 million people install Android apps outside the Google store. (That’s excluding China and things like the Samsung and Epic Games Stores.) The biggest reasons are (i) piracy, (ii) modified YouTube/Spotify/WhatsApp clients, (iii) region-locked games, (iv) forbidden gambling or crypto apps, (v) local sharing to save on mobile data, and (vi; least common) open-source app repositories like F-Droid.
In an escalated lockdown, some of this might still be allowed, e.g. local sharing. And many people would simply accept the new restrictions. But I expect that a substantial number would suddenly become interested in de-Googled Android variants that don’t enforce the lockdown. That would be dangerous for Google: If a significant fraction of those 300-500 million people switched, there’s a risk of a vicious/virtuous cycle, where people tell their friends, manufacturers start to cater to those variants, and so on.
If that happened, what would Google do? Might they clamp down on those Android variants, too? Again, maybe! Technically, Android is open-source, but if Google really wanted to kill Lineage or Graphene, there are about 200 different ways they could do that.
So say they did. What would the people currently using those variants do? Again, many would simply submit. That’s good for Google. Others would decide that if they must have an overlord, they’d prefer Apple. That’s not good for Google, but probably not a huge problem given the numbers. But others would decide to look elsewhere, likely to true Linux phones.
Currently, it’s estimated that less than 100 thousand people daily-drive true Linux phones, 30-50 times less than the number of people who use de-Googled Android variants. I’m too lazy and selfish to use a Linux phone now, but Google will take my RSS app from my cold dead hands, so in this scenario, I’d likely switch. If a fraction of people do that—or even get a second Linux phone—it would still represent a huge infusion of money and energy into the Linux phone ecosystem. If this pushed Linux phones from “bad” to “sort of OK”, that could kick off a growth cycle. Eventually, there would be a risk that Europe—eager to decouple from an unreliable US—might embrace them by mandating that government employees use them, or passing a law that popular apps must provide a web-app version that works on Linux phones, or whatever.
Would that actually happen? I don’t know, but neither does Google. My point is that the downside risk of losing their phone duopoly seems vastly larger than the upside, so why risk it? The smart move is to crush alternative app stores and fight malicious apps while making the bare minimum concessions to keep the freedom and privacy people onside. That’s exactly what what Google appears to be doing.
Of course, they might go for a full lockdown anyway. Corporations do dumb things all the time. But I really don’t see how it would be in their self-interest, and I’m not sure it would be a bad thing if they did.
Dynomight: could google achieve the security aims of the android lockdown without so much harm to freedom or privacy
Google Gemini 4: Yes. Security experts, privacy advocates, and open-source developers widely agree that Google’s primary security objectives—protecting users from malware, financial fraud, spyware, and social engineering—can be achieved through architectural containment, transparent auditing, and informed consent rather than centralized gatekeeping and surveillance. […] The reason Google chooses centralized lockdown over user-controlled security is largely economic and strategic, not technical:
Ecosystem Lock-in: Tying security APIs (like Play Integrity) to Google Play Services makes it nearly impossible for competitors or open-source forks to build a viable alternative Android ecosystem that supports banking and media apps.
Advertising Revenue: Features that dramatically improve both security and privacy—like a native network firewall, revocable internet permissions, or frictionless support for system-wide ad blockers—directly threaten Google’s primary revenue stream.
Liability & Support Reduction: Treating all users as untrusted and removing root/power-user capabilities reduces the surface area of user error, even if it removes the user’s ownership of their own hardware.

America cannot undo Trumpism (permalink) True Carneyism has never been tried. When Canadian PM Mark Carney traveled to Davos to declare a "rupture" in the old order (and admit that this old order was never that great to begin with) he told us that there was no going back from Trumpism. The only way out of Trumpism was through: https://www.weforum.org/stories/forum-institutional/davos-2026-special-address-by-mark-carney-prime-minister-of-canada/ This is easy to say, but hard to do. If the old order is over, then we will never again be able to trust America to serve as the world's cop, banker, ISP, IT department and consumer of first resort. We can't trust Americans to buy the things we make: https://pluralistic.net/2025/12/16/k-shaped-recovery/#disenshittification-nations We can't trust them not to interfere with the interconnections between fiber lines that slither out of the oceans and onto the US landmass: https://pluralistic.net/2025/11/26/difficult-multipolarism/#eurostack We can't trust them not to weaponize the US dollar to undermine sovereign nations' legitimate activities: https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/26/i-dont-want/#your-greenback-dollar And we absolutely can't trust them not to spy on, steal from, and shut down governments, firms and households around the world by cutting off access to US software and cloud services, and by bricking the world's devices, from tractors to smartphones: https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/01/39c3/#the-new-coalition Despite Carney's assertion that this rupture represents a welcome (if too cruel, sudden and painful) departure of the old (never very good) system, no one (not even Carney) is acting like the world has truly changed. Take Carney's answer to the Trump tariffs: retaliatory tariffs. Tariffs have a place in sheltering a nascent domestic industry from better-developed, deeper-pocketed foreign competitors, so a tariff wall between Canada and the US could make sense, if it was paired with the massive domestic investment we'd need to rebuild the manufacturing industry that Brian Mulroney sold out with the Canada-US Free Trade Agreement (and later NAFTA). But Carney is no Carneyist. When it comes to massive domestic spending, Carney is a bog-standard, austerity-addled Reaganomics guy; a central banker and technocrat whose idea of "industrial policy" is firing tens of thousands of skilled civil servants who thwart his agenda and replacing them with defective (but obedient) chatbots running on US hardware: https://pluralistic.net/2026/05/13/vibe-governance/#k-hole Carney's retaliatory tariffs aren't what you'd do if the old order had "ruptured." They're what you'd do if you hoped that your American cousins would come to their senses, evict their mad king from the White House, tear down the Epstein Memorial Ballroom, and roll back the clock to 2016. Like a lot of liberals, Carney just wants to go back to brunch. But as any true Carneyist knows, brunch is canceled forever. Brunch ruptured. There's no going back to the old America, and there's no going back to the old American order that had dominated the world since the end of WWII. As November Kelly says, "Trump inherited a poker game rigged in his favor, but he flipped the table over anyway because he resented having to pretend to play." This is something we're all struggling with, including Americans. The Republicans' midterm wipeout has corporate Democrats hoping that after a few years' tinkering, they can elect a Newsomdroid or give Harris a do-over and win back the trust and reliance of the world and the American people. Even for a true Carneyist who never liked the old order very much (like me), this is a comforting prospect. No one knows what the next world will look like, and no matter how screwed up the old world was, I knew how it worked and how to make it work for me (more or less). But there is no going back. Trump I didn't have a plan, it only had Trump, whose One Big Idea was issuing Executive Orders. Many of these were meaningless bloviating. Some were illegal and were swiftly suspended or never went into effect. Biden overturned nearly all the remaining EOs (that were both substantive and not totally illegal). But Trump II had Project 2025. The point of Project 2025 and the ambition of the wreckers who wrote it was to push America through a series of one-way transformations that cannot be undone, and that's what's happened, over two short years. That's the bad news. The good news is that it's much easier to destroy than to build, so Project 2025 hasn't led to the creation of permanent, load-bearing fascist institutions that cannot be shuttered without bringing down large parts of the USA. Start with values. Trumpism is a denial of democracy and the rule of law. Tens of millions of Americans have been marinated in a belief system that says that the way to win power is to claim all the elections you lose are rigged and that these "stolen elections" are best addressed by staging a coup. These people are in a cult that embraces its leader's naked corruption. They're in a cult whose doctrine treats political triumph of as divine direction to embark on looting sprees. It's a cult whose members mutilate their faces so that they can't ever leave, and the reward for this permanent disfigurement is endless influence-peddling: https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/6136101-ambassador-guilfoyle-wire-request/ Even without ritual scarification to mark them out forever, millions of these people will never come back from this cult indoctrination. They will forever be democracy's enemies, treating the idea of laws, rules and honest service as shucks for the rubes. What's more, these people's neighbors, family members and co-workers will never be able to fully trust them. Unfortunately, those values aren't just diffused through the population: they are concentrated in the organs of state. DOGE and Federalist Society judicial appointments have created a stay-behind cadre of life-tenured fascists who now dominate America's federal judiciary and permanent civil service, including and especially the nation's law enforcement and national security agencies, from the FBI to the FDA, the NSA to the Bureau of Prisons. Worse: DOGE also chased away hundreds of thousands of skilled, principled public servants. Those people have retired, retrained, emigrated or exited the workforce. They can't simply be re-hired and restored to their old roles. From finance regulation to the national education system, America has lobotomized itself, swapping people who understand how things work and use that understanding to enforce the laws and safeguard the American people for end-times fascists, caliper-wielding eugenicists, and Ayn Rand LARPers. Much of the work DOGE's victims did is also gone forever. When DOGE's muskrats killed long-running NIH research projects, they pulled the plug on studies, some of which had run for decades. Many of these experiments are unsalvageable. DOGE didn't just throw away the contributions that cancer patients, people with genetic disorders and other volunteer research subjects gave to science: in halting these research projects, DOGE shredded this selfless sacrifice. Why not? When one NIH official begged his DOGE invaders not to kill long-running, valuable cancer research, the DOGE child laughed and said it didn't matter, because AI was going to cure cancer. Then there's the NIH's research partners: the elite institutions who buckled so quickly in the face of Trump's antisemitism/DEI witch-hunts. These universities now face the same crisis as the DOGE-gutted civil service, with their best and brightest gone, grad students chased back to their home countries, and the trust of their students and faculty permanently squandered. It's not just grad students who got chased out of America. Immigrants – documented and undocumented alike – have been terrorized for two years and many of them have fled. ICE got what it wanted: they robbed aging, stagnant America of the dynamism, aspiration and youthful vigor of the most ambitious people from every corner of the globe, people who proved their resourcefulness and bravery by making dangerous crossings. Then they navigated the US immigration system's impenetrable bureaucracy, often working without legal representation, in a language they were just learning, and still managing to clear every bureaucratic hurdle. This alone is a breathtaking demonstration of intelligence, resourcefulness and diligence. Those brilliant, hardworking people aren't coming back: some other country will get the benefit of their life's work and care. Their children will become citizens of other nations. Now think of the hundreds of billions of dollars that have been transferred from ordinary working people who are still here, to America's oligarchs. Trump's tax cuts, corrupt policy subsidies and no-bid pork contracts have supercharged the wealth (and thus the power) of America's most corrupt elite. It will be the work of a generation to tax away their stolen loot, and much of it may never be recovered. These people will spend that time working to transform their wealth into permanent power, buying and installing politicians at every level of office. Trumpland is a coalition of wreckers of every kind. Think of how MAHA undermined the nation's herd immunity to a host of communicable diseases, many of which can result in permanent disability. Long after MAHA is forgotten even as a punchline, the people whose health they destroyed forever will still be struggling. After a century of painstaking work to corral measles and other killer diseases, MAHA immunocompromised America itself, in just two short years. Any attempt to bring back evidence-based preventative medicine must now overcome the deep mistrust of medical science that an army of supplement-peddling quacks has sunk deep into Americans' psyche. Speaking of mistrust: Americans must now and forever live with the knowledge that tens of thousands of their neighbors joined ICE, an armed, masked kidnapping squad that occupied US cities, murdering US citizens and noncitizens alike in the streets with impunity. Even if we try and imprison every one of those war criminals, it will take years and will shatter families and communities. ICE proved that America is awash in small arms, but it's a different story when it comes to significant warfighting materiel. Trump's Iranian disaster used up the largest part of Pax Americana's arsenal of missiles and anti-missile interceptors. Putin doesn't need to convince Trump to cut off Ukraine's access to America's long-range arsenal. Trump shot his wad, and re-arming America is the work of decades, and it will cost billions, and it will require access to things America no longer knows how to make. Worse: the places where they do know how to make those things are no longer America's allies. Can they be America's allies again? Well, sure, but only in a limited, Carneyist, "minilateral" way, in which countries form temporary alliances to accomplish specific goals. Biden spoke of "friendshoring" production of key goods and services. Friendshoring implies a reliable form of friendship, the sort that is built on decades of trust and interdependence. Friendshoring only works if the friends you friendshore to can be relied upon to stay your friends. Do we really think that if Venezuela deposes the puppet regime Trump installed after kidnapping the country's leader that it will remain America's "friend?" That's the problem with weaponized interdependence: it only works for so long as the country America is screwing remains dependent on America, and now every country in the world is moving heaven and earth to break their dependencies on America, its institutions and products: https://pluralistic.net/2023/10/10/weaponized-interdependence/#the-other-swifties As Nate Bethea says on this week's Trashfuture podcast, airports outside of the USA are now filled with large, splashy ads urging businesses to move their IT out of America's cloud and off of American apps: https://pluralistic.net/2023/10/10/weaponized-interdependence/#the-other-swifties After Microsoft obliged the Trump regime by taking away the online accounts of foreign officials who made Trump angry, will any other country ever voluntarily trust them with their industrial capacity, let alone their government? https://www.forbes.com/sites/emmawoollacott/2025/07/22/microsoft-cant-keep-eu-data-safe-from-us-authorities/ I'm not saying America is a write-off: I'm saying that it has been sabotaged down to the foundation slab and structural members by a psychotic cadre of skilled arsonists, who were abetted by mad bombers who drove themselves even crazier by racking up life-altering debts in rigged "prediction markets" that serve as a vehicle for bankrupting yourself by wishcasting away your life's savings by betting on every aspect of a Permanent Chud Reich, as corrupt officials make out like bandits by trading on insider information. When America comes back (if America comes back), it will not be as the organizing platform for the world's finance, military, technology and commerce. In years or perhaps decades, America may find a new stable place in the international community. But in the meantime, it cannot be relied upon to serve as the world's hyperpower. Trump forever disqualified America from enjoying that privileged place – and just to be sure, he destroyed its capacity to even try. articles.title: AI and Irontown
articles.summary:
For our last movie night we watched Princess
Mononoke.  I remembered loving
that movie when I was younger, but watching it as an adult made me once again
realize how Miyazaki has a way of expressing diverging sides without picking
one.  The film shows people, animals and spirits with legitimate and largely
incompatible needs, and each faction is further engaged in infighting.
A central arc of the story is Lady Eboshi’s Irontown, which gives people who
were largely rejected by society work, protection and dignity.  She gives
shelter and work to those who have leprosy and to former sex workers.  The mine
and the weapon factory provide them with a livelihood, but they also destroy the
forest around them.  The forest’s inhabitants, in particular the boars,
response choose war against the humans to defend themselves.  Eboshi is not
portrayed as a villain.  She does real good for the people of Irontown, but
also is an arms manufacturer who is destroying the forest around it.
The film anchors around a character called Ashitaka, who has been condemned to
death by an unfortunate encounter with a god that was turned into a demon after
being fatally wounded by one of Eboshi’s guns.  He doesn’t take sides, but he
wants to understand and find the truth.  Another character is San (whom they
call Mononoke), a girl who was raised by wolves and, despite being human,
considers herself part of the forest.
This movie’s backdrop is human progress, and it reminded me so much of the
challenges we are facing today with AI.  AI is useful, empowering and
consequential beyond the people who benefit from it.  It’s similar to the iron
in the story.  Irontown gives the outcast purpose and power.  There are people
today who see themselves in an environment just like that: people who were
never let in before and who can now build things that were out of reach.  They
are wielding AI to their benefit.  But there are negative externalities.  In
Mononoke it’s not just the spirits and animals in the forest who bear the
consequences, it’s also other people.  Irontown produces guns, and its people
are engaged in fights with other humans.  There is conflict and power seeking
everywhere.
Another, unseen character is the power-hungry emperor, who wants the head of
the forest spirit, a god, because he believes it will make him immortal.
Eboshi is willing to support that cause, not because she thinks it’s right, but
because she is at war with the forest’s gods who are preventing her expansion,
so they have a common interest.  But there really is no need for anyone to kill
the forest spirit, in the same way there is no need for any one country to “win
at AI”.  What drives it is the fear of what happens if someone else wins first.
And the emperor is willing to have a god killed for it.  The people who help him
with that desire, Eboshi included, don’t understand the chaos it will unleash.
There it also shows the dangers of seeking overwhelming power without
comprehension of how to control its consequences.  The pursuit of power itself
becomes destructive.  In the end, the gods die, and what grows back is not the
old forest anymore.  Irontown is destroyed.  Eboshi wants to rebuild it, and to
build a better town this time.  Ashitaka stays with the people of Irontown after
his curse is lifted by the dying forest spirit.  San cannot forgive the humans
and stays with the wolves.  In the end, nothing is truly resolved, but there is
a truce that came at great cost.
Ashitaka’s role in the movie is one of a neutral actor.  He was wronged both by
a spirit turned demon in the forest, who put a curse on him, and, indirectly, by
Eboshi, who caused the spirit to turn evil.  Yet he harbors no ill will towards
either side.  He sets out to “see with eyes unclouded by hate,” and in the
course of the movie he is seen as an unaligned actor.  He helps people on both
sides, and stands in their way to prevent further conflict.  He doesn’t feel
like a pacifist, but he’s the closest to one there is.  He’s a truth seeker in
a changing world.  Because he engages he’s
seen as suspicious by both sides, and ends up shot by the people of Irontown
when he tries to rescue San.
I use AI every day and find it genuinely empowering.  But I also recognize the
pain it causes some, and the moral problems it poses.  It’s genuine progress
for humanity, but it comes at significant cost.  And many of those costs will be
carried by people who aren’t going to benefit from it.
So it’s no surprise that AI feels like a threat to many today.  Communities
currently strongly align themselves with one
side and fight against the other.  The forst spirit did not have to die and the
boars did not have to die in a senseless war.
The question is not whether there will be iron, but what kind of Irontown we
build with it.  I want our conversation about AI to make room for nuance and
genuine understanding, for us to look at it and each other with eyes unclouded
by hate.  We should take advantage of its real benefits, but also recognize the
damage it can do, and the choices we still have about what we build and what
we’re willing to sacrifice for it.  I like to think there is a path for people
with differing opinions can find a way to live alongside before losing something
we can’t get back.

articles.title: Introducing Ninety
articles.summary:
We’re excited to announce Ninety, the first prediction market for open source security, launching today in partnership with Lanternfish, the frontier AI lab for software security. Security report volumes at major projects are four to five times higher than in 2024. Attackers and defenders are both running frontier models against the same few thousand packages, and everything those models turn up is scattered across disclosure inboxes, private chats, embargo lists and exploit brokers, with no price attached.
Ninety puts a price on it. Anyone can take a position on whether an open source project will have a vulnerability disclosed, how severe it will be, and how long the fix will take. Researchers earn from the markets they called correctly, and defenders who harden code earn when contracts resolve NO. Everyone who depends on open source gets a per-project price for how secure their dependencies are, updated every second.
Rationale
Bug bounties make one payment to whoever finds a bug, after the report is in. Grant programs fund a handful of projects a year after a long application process. Both fall behind when a single model run can produce forty plausible reports before lunch, and this year several bounties closed. curl ended its bug bounty in January and Google paused its open source VRP in October, citing “a significant rise in automated submissions, the vast majority of which are not valid.” HackerOne’s Internet Bug Bounty paused new submissions and cut its medium-severity payout from $1,843 to $297. Ninety replaces the submission queue with an order book, and every new report moves the price.
Writing about curl’s bug bounty in 2024, Daniel Stenberg called it “an absolute and undisputed success”. Ninety takes the same incentive and makes it continuous and open to anyone with a verified account.
Mechanics
Each market is a binary contract on a single project over a fixed window. The standard term is ninety days, matching the industry disclosure deadline and giving Ninety its name. Contracts trade between $0 and $1, and the price is the traders’ current estimate of the probability that the event happens. Launch markets include:
curl: Will a CVE rated High or Critical be published before 31 January 2027?
OpenSSL: Will the next major release ship before the next High-severity advisory?
Linux: Over/under on kernel CVEs published in December, line set by Lanternfish.
lodash: Will the maintainers respond to the next security report within 14 days?
PHP: Will a follow-up fix for php2shell be needed before 1 February 2027?
Every listed project also has a set of standard side markets: days-to-patch, whether a fix gets backported to older release lines, whether the advisory gets a name and a logo, and whether the repository is archived or its sole maintainer steps down before expiry.
Contracts can be chained into parlays, which pay out when every leg resolves YES, with odds set by Lanternfish. A dependency parlay has a leg for each step of a fix through the graph, such as a High-severity advisory in zlib followed by a CVE for each listed project that vendors it. The most popular parlay in beta was the Long Weekend, with legs for a Critical CVE published on a Friday, the first fix released after Monday, and the sole maintainer stepping down within the contract window.
Results
Ninety has been in private beta with a few hundred traders since the summer. The PHP “CVSS 9+ before Halloween” contract traded at four cents for most of September. It closed at 97 cents on the afternoon of 20 October, the day before PHP shipped fixes for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and CISA’s addition of both to the KEV catalog on 26 October settled the follow-on exploitation contract. Congratulations to whoever was buying in September.
Our most traded contract of the year is the exploit count over/under on Copy Fail, the Linux kernel privilege escalation found with AI assistance in April. It resolved at 132 public proofs of concept.
Backtested against historical data, the 2024 xz-utils backdoor would have been the most profitable position in open source history. The account best placed to take it had commit access to the project and would have been barred under our insider rules.
“I used to send reports to maintainers and wait months for a reply,” said Max Tokens, the top-earning YES trader in the beta. “These days I buy YES on the project first and then file the report.”
“We run Lanternfish against every project we hold NO on, and the returns cover the compute,” said Ram Hoarder, who leads a four-person defensive trading desk on the NO side. “Patches go into our fork until the contract expires, which protects the position.”
Lanternfish
Ninety is sponsored by Lanternfish, whose models are used by most of the researchers who find open source vulnerabilities and most of the teams who fix them. Every verified trader gets Lanternfish credits on signup. Lanternfish is Ninety’s designated market maker and provides liquidity on both sides of every contract. On the Copy Fail over/under it made the market on both sides while traders using its models generated most of the 132 proofs of concept being counted. Each of those model runs counted toward the Security Investment Score of the trader who ran it, which tracks Lanternfish usage and is shown on their public profile next to their returns.
“Security in 2026 is a compute problem,” said Chip Shortage, CEO of Lanternfish. “Attackers are using frontier models to find bugs, so defenders have to use them too, and Ninety pays both sides back for the compute.”
Integrity
Ninety has strict insider rules to keep prices fair. Trading on a project is blocked for anyone with commit, release or publish access to it, anyone named in its maintainers file, code owners or security policy, and anyone who received an embargoed report about it in the last twelve months. We match identities against commit history, registry ownership records and signing keys automatically, so maintainers are excluded without signing up. “Maintainers are excluded the day their project is listed,” said Chuck Sum, Ninety’s Head of Market Integrity. “Most of them have no idea Ninety exists, which is exactly what you want from an insider control.”
A trader who opens a pull request against a listed project becomes an insider for that project when the pull request is opened, and their positions are closed at the current price. Most traders hold fixes in a private fork until their contracts expire.
Maintainers know more about their own projects than anyone else, so they’re the one group permanently excluded. We expect most of them to be fine with that. As Daniel Stenberg wrote earlier this year, “I am not in this game for the money or the extravagant life style.”
Traders may research the projects they hold positions in, including submitting security reports, requesting CVEs, opening issues, and asking for status updates on existing reports. Any contact with a maintainer intended to influence a market outcome must be disclosed on the trader’s profile within 24 hours.
Markets resolve when any CNA publishes a CVE record for the project, and resolution is based on publication alone. Records that are later disputed or rejected still resolve YES if they were published inside the contract window.
Listing
Any project with a package on a major registry and at least one CVE in its history is listed automatically. Ninety lists projects without asking their maintainers, because the security of widely used software is a matter of public interest and the markets reflect information that already exists.
Maintainers can request delisting from any market page. A delisting request is material non-public information about the project, so it’s disclosed to traders as soon as it’s received and marked on the price chart. Archiving a repository settles that project’s abandonment markets, and its other markets run to expiry.
0.1% of all trading fees go into the Maintainer Appreciation Pool, paid out quarterly to the maintainers of listed projects as Lanternfish credits, with the largest shares going to projects whose markets resolve NO most often. Credits can be spent on Lanternfish’s report triage models. Each listed project also gets one complimentary read-only dashboard seat, and maintainers can apply for delayed market data on their own projects, released ninety days after each contract settles.
Organisations
Teams can buy YES across their dependency tree as a hedge, so a critical CVE in a transitive dependency pays out when your exposure is highest, and for most organisations a hedged dependency tree costs less than a support contract. “We moved our open source sponsorship budget into a YES position across our whole dependency tree,” said Audrey Trail, CISO at a Fortune 100 retailer. “It’s paid out four times this year.”
Upload an SPDX or CycloneDX SBOM and Ninety builds the hedge for you. Each listed component gets its own YES contract. Teams now have a financial reason to update the SBOM whenever a dependency changes.
Since 11 September, manufacturers selling into the EU have had to report actively exploited vulnerabilities under the Cyber Resilience Act. The early warning is due within 24 hours. Ninety’s CRA hedge adds an exploitation contract for every component in your SBOM. Each position is sized to the Act’s maximum fine: €15 million or 2.5% of worldwide turnover, whichever is higher. When one of your dependencies is exploited, the payout arrives before your early warning is due.
The Ninety price feed is available to software composition analysis vendors as a per-package security signal, and procurement teams can set a minimum NO price for any dependency entering their software.
Availability
Ninety is live today in 41 jurisdictions. Sign up, verify your identity, and connect a Lanternfish key. Your first ten trades are free. Know the odds.
If you maintain a listed project, thank you for creating value for the Ninety ecosystem.
Editor’s note: This is satire, not a product spec. Please don’t build it. How to Ruin All of Package Management covers what happens when markets get attached to open source metrics. If you have money for open source security, give it to the projects. Daniel Stenberg’s The pressure describes the current volume of reports from the receiving end.

articles.title: Yak-Shaving Overload
articles.summary:
Over the years I’ve gotten myself into all varieties of technical rabbit holes and wild goose chases. But I’m feeling weird about my latest trip, involving a forgotten Linux tablet. I blame AI.

Recently, I took on a project that I thought would be a lot of fun … but in the end, I did not like how it made me feel. And I think it reflects the real dangers of leaning too aggressively on AI for stuff you’d like to try out.
A quick explainer: About four years ago, I got a hold of a JingPad, a Linux-based tablet with a massive Achilles’ heel. The problem? It was sold as a Linux-first tablet on ARM, but it was built around an SoC that was not actually particularly open. The Unisoc Tiger T510, as I’ve written, was built for Android, and it has PowerVR graphics that didn’t have an open-source driver. Worse, the company that made it disappeared off the face of the Earth just a handful of months after it first appeared.
The JingPad was a working, fully functional tablet that had been done dirty by its ownership and a bad engineering decision. It was a perfect candidate for the very kind of deconstruction project that has been taking the internet by storm in recent weeks.
So, my goal was this: Let’s see if I can use Claude, Deepseek, Xiaomi MiMo, and other LLMs to get this dang thing working in a modern version of Linux. Certain components, namely the proprietary GPU, might prove difficult, but using Ghidra, Reverse Engineer Anything (REA), and a willing-to-go-at-it LLM, it could take things down the road for me.
How hard could it be?

The good, and bad, of an insane yak-shaving project
This is an example of yak-shaving, a concept in which one project gradually evolves into numerous complex branches that never seem to end. For those not familiar, it is based on a Ren & Stimpy skit called “Yak Shaving Day,” which I’ve helpfully embedded above.
Tech projects have a tendency to devolve into wild goose chases like this, as hinted above, but this was a whole new beast to me.
Anyway, I want to make clear that this project wasn’t an outright failure. From literally nothing but an empty boot screen, we got the device to load a relatively modern version of Fedora on a “dirty” Linux kernel, based on 6.18. In many ways, it worked, complete with a working touchscreen screen, a charging battery, WiFi access, and an accessible GNOME interface. While not especially fast, I believe it is about as stable as JingOS, the software that came on it in 2022 and itself did not have GPU accelerated graphics.
There were even fun quirks that emerged as I was working on this. I got the flashlight for the camera working on the back, even though there’s literally no use case where it’d actually be useful. And I made significant progress adding FM radio support for the device, despite the fact that, like most mobile devices, FM radio support was never an actual feature of the tool. (In both cases, I thought it would be funny, even though the joke was honestly limited to just me.)
Unfortunately, getting to this point created a project that I would best describe as all-consuming. I had a swarm of different agents going at different components, different parts of the device, attempting to scrape details from old firmware versions and related projects in the hope that it’d uncover something missed previously. The result: I had to baby the damn thing all day, managing a bunch of LLMs and rebooting the device as the agents I was using went down one dead-end after another. And shockingly, the thing that kind of made the process less fun and more of a quagmire? It wasn’t the GPU, as I expected; it was the sound.
I got as far as having all the components of the sound card separately working; the DMA chip, the speakers, the codecs, and so on. The GNOME settings app even recognized that the sound card was there. But after receiving something like 50 “this is the last thing before you finally hear sound” messages from DeepSeek, I realized that I had gotten my own brain into a dangerous loop. It was nonstop dopamine hit on top of nonstop dopamine hit—the promise of instant gratification without getting gratified—and after a while, I kind of just felt mentally drained by it all.
This was a “me” project, one that I wanted to see in the world, but in the end it was kind of getting in the way of me thinking about literally anything else.
The way I broke the chain, at least for now, was simple: I put the tablet away for now. I’m going to try my best to get a healthy distance from it. If and when I come back to this project, I want to ensure I’m doing it for reasons that help me learn something rather than stress me out.


Evidence that, yes, I did get Fedora working on my JingPad.
In the right context, things like this can be good
This all sounds like a dangerous hobby. But to make the counterargument: For years, we’ve heard stories about smart devices and other objects losing support over time because a company shut down a server somewhere, or chose not to modernize them. With moves like these, we can revive these devices.
For example, the seemingly dead Hackintosh scene has actually seen signs of life, thanks to AI. There’s now a driver for modern-day Nvidia cards on Intel Hackintoshes. It is now possible to boot MacOS on a Snapdragon PC. And Cutefish, a new MacOS-like distro, has promised something previously thought impossible—working graphical MacOS apps in a Linux environment.
A decade ago, when Hackintosh was hitting its peak point in popularity, all this stuff was crazy talk. No way was this going to happen.
And to be clear, there have been other projects I’ve tried that went way better than the one above. As I recently wrote in Boxed News, I was able to turn Dux Shell (formerly Dank Material Shell) into a usable TV computing experience.
Yes, AI is capable of reshaping computing experiences in new ways, in ways that some might find culturally frustrating if the reason you get into tech is because of specific scenes. (I personally don’t, and think the line between cool stuff and gatekeeping is quite small.)
But I’m personally of the view that in cases like the JingPad, where this tablet would be sitting around being useless otherwise, stuff like REA could have genuine value. After all, even if I don’t end up using it to type the next Great American blog post, it can still be useful as a makeshift self-hosting device or even just a lightweight way to surf the web. And I’m hopeful that, eventually, I’ll turn this into a feature-complete device, even with the components that Unisoc and Imagination didn’t bother to make public. However …

Shave yaks? If you value your mental health, pace yourself
If there’s anything I’ve learned about myself over the past decade, I get sucked into different directions way too easily. I can get obsessed with things, and that obsession can sometimes lead to cool places. (See &udm=14.)
But something about the process of attempting to use AI to fix an old tablet felt kind of damaging to a routine in a way that few of my hobbies have over the years. I mentioned Hackintoshing before, and honestly that’s kind of what it reminds me of the most, this attempt to make something do a thing it was never meant to do. But when so much of what you’re doing is working up against something hyping up every action, it’s hard not to feel hollow at the end of it.
As is highlighted by the fact that I publish a little less often these days, I don’t use AI for any of my actual writing. I try taking my time with it. But in a world where it seems like AI is the decorative bird of technology, it can intrude in dangerous ways, with costs that don’t necessarily show themselves right away. And I’m not talking about tokens.
I’m a well-known yak shaver. It’s what I do. This newsletter is a shrine to yak-shaving at the end of the day. But I did not like the way I felt at the end of this week, having hit the reset button on the JingPad for the 250th time. I’m sure I’m not alone here.
My suggestion to anyone else who yak-shaves: Approach agents with caution. After all, an AI agent does not have a limit; you do. Projects like these only take and take your energy, and leave you with a broken-feeling brain.
And unlike a static code window or a page of docs, an agent can make false claims or hype up promises it can’t back up.
